subject: biology

items.q: Which statement correctly applies the term organelle as it is used in IB Biology?
items.correct: The plasma membrane is an organelle, although it forms the boundary of the cytoplasm.
items.misconception: Ribosomes are not organelles, because they are not bounded by a membrane.
items.why: Many textbooks and pre-IB courses define an organelle as 'a membrane-bound structure', and ribosomes are then presented as an exception or left out, so students carry the membrane requirement into IB Biology. The IB definition is based on function, not on a membrane: an organelle is a discrete subunit adapted to a specific function. Ribosomes, vesicles, nuclei and the plasma membrane are all organelles; the cell wall, cytoskeleton and cytoplasm are not.
items.specStatementText: What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found
items.random_wrong: The cell wall is an organelle, because it is a labelled part with a function.

items.q: Liver cells were broken open in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution and the homogenate was spun in an ultracentrifuge at a series of increasing speeds. Only the pellet formed at the second speed consumed oxygen and produced ATP when supplied with substrates. What does this investigation illustrate about how progress in science is made?
items.correct: A technique for isolating one type of organelle made it possible to test its function directly, which could not be done before.
items.misconception: Electron micrographs of the organelles in the second pellet would have revealed the same function, so the centrifuge added little that was new.
items.why: Structure and function are always taught together, and the electron microscope is remembered as the technique that revealed organelles, so students assume that seeing a structure in detail also revealed what it does. An electron micrograph shows structure, not activity. The function of a mitochondrion or a ribosome was established by isolating that organelle in an ultracentrifuge and showing, for example, that the isolated fraction consumed oxygen or made protein. Progress in science often follows the development of a new technique in this way.
items.specStatementText: What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found
items.random_wrong: The ATP must have come from intact cells surviving in the pellet, since organelles cannot work once removed from a cell.

items.q: In a eukaryotic cell, newly transcribed RNA is modified in the nucleus before it is translated. How does the separation of the nucleus from the cytoplasm make this possible?
items.correct: Translation happens only in the cytoplasm, so the RNA cannot meet a ribosome until modified and out through a pore.
items.misconception: Ribosomes inside the nucleus translate the RNA while it is being modified, so the two processes run together in the same place.
items.why: Pre-IB courses describe the nucleus as 'controlling the cell' and as the place where genetic information is used, and students have not yet separated transcription (in the nucleus) from translation (in the cytoplasm). Transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm. The nuclear membrane keeps newly made mRNA away from ribosomes, which is what allows the mRNA to be modified before it is translated. This separation is the advantage of having a nucleus that the guide identifies.
items.specStatementText: Why keep the nucleus and cytoplasm apart
items.random_wrong: The nuclear membrane keeps the ribosomes away from the DNA, which they would otherwise translate directly into protein.

items.q: A gene from a eukaryote is inserted into a bacterium and is transcribed there. In the eukaryotic cell the mRNA from this gene would be modified before translation. What happens to the mRNA in the bacterium?
items.correct: It is translated at once, without any modification.
items.misconception: It is modified in the cytoplasm before ribosomes can bind it.
items.why: Transcription and translation are taught as a single universal pathway from gene to protein, so any step learned for eukaryotes is assumed to apply to every cell. Post-transcriptional modification of mRNA is possible in eukaryotes because the nucleus separates transcription from translation. In prokaryotes this is not possible: ribosomes attach to the mRNA as soon as it emerges from RNA polymerase, so there is no opportunity to modify it first.
items.specStatementText: Why keep the nucleus and cytoplasm apart
items.random_wrong: It is translated inside the nucleoid before it is released.

items.q: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes at a concentration far higher than in the surrounding cytoplasm. Why is keeping these enzymes inside a lysosome an advantage to the cell?
items.correct: The enzymes are concentrated where they are needed and kept apart from the cytoplasm, whose contents they would otherwise hydrolyse.
items.misconception: The membrane merely stores the enzymes, since their specificity would stop them harming the cell if they escaped.
items.why: Enzyme specificity is learned as 'one enzyme, one substrate' and is taken to mean that an enzyme only acts on the thing it is meant to act on, rather than on any molecule of the right type. Lysosomal enzymes are specific to types of bond, such as peptide bonds, which are found in every protein in the cell. Keeping them inside a lysosome separates a biochemical process, hydrolysis, from the rest of the cell's contents, with which it is incompatible. This separation of incompatible processes is one of the advantages of compartmentalization.
items.specStatementText: Why compartments help the cytoplasm
items.random_wrong: The membrane slows hydrolysis to a safe rate by limiting how fast substrates can reach the enzymes inside.

items.q: A phagocyte engulfs a bacterium into a phagocytic vacuole, and lysosomes then fuse with the vacuole. What is the advantage of digesting the bacterium inside this compartment rather than in the cytoplasm?
items.correct: Hydrolytic enzymes reach a high concentration around the bacterium while being unable to digest the phagocyte's own contents.
items.misconception: The vacuole makes its own enzymes on its membrane, so the lysosomes only add more membrane to enlarge it.
items.why: Lysosomes are described as 'digestive organelles' that 'contain enzymes', and students slide from 'contains' to 'produces', especially as the organelle that actually makes the enzymes is not mentioned alongside it. Neither lysosomes nor phagocytic vacuoles contain ribosomes, so they cannot make protein. Hydrolytic enzymes are made on the rough endoplasmic reticulum and packaged by the Golgi apparatus into lysosomes. A phagocytic vacuole has no enzymes of its own until lysosomes fuse with it, which is why that fusion is essential for digestion.
items.specStatementText: Why compartments help the cytoplasm
items.random_wrong: The enzymes could safely be released anywhere in the cell, so the vacuole serves only to hold the bacterium still.

items.q: During aerobic cell respiration the electron transport chain pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space of the mitochondrion. Why is the small volume of the intermembrane space an adaptation for ATP production?
items.correct: Few protons need to be pumped to produce a steep concentration gradient, so the gradient forms quickly.
items.misconception: Its volume is not itself an adaptation: it is the total number of protons stored that determines the ATP yield.
items.why: Students think of the space as a reservoir whose capacity matters, rather than of the concentration difference across the membrane, and 'more of something' is assumed to be better. ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis is driven by the concentration gradient of protons across the inner membrane, not by the total number stored. A small intermembrane volume means that each proton pumped raises the concentration by more, so the gradient becomes steep with fewer protons pumped and ATP synthesis begins sooner.
items.specStatementText: How a mitochondrion is built for ATP (HL)
items.random_wrong: It brings oxygen entering through the outer membrane close to the cristae, which absorb it for use in respiration.

items.q: Electron micrographs of mitochondria from two tissues were analysed. In tissue X the inner membrane had an area of about 40 µm² per µm³ of mitochondrial volume; in tissue Y the value was about 15 µm² per µm³. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
items.correct: Mitochondria in tissue X hold more electron transport chains and ATP synthase per unit volume.
items.misconception: Mitochondria in tissue X absorb oxygen and glucose more quickly through their more extensive cristae.
items.why: Pre-IB courses use 'large surface area' almost exclusively for absorption (root hairs, villi, alveoli), so students apply the same explanation to any folded surface they meet. The cristae are folds of the inner membrane, not of the outer surface, so they do not increase the area available for uptake into the mitochondrion. Their large area is an adaptation for the processes that happen in the inner membrane: electron transport, proton pumping and ATP synthesis.
items.specStatementText: How a mitochondrion is built for ATP (HL)
items.random_wrong: Mitochondria in tissue X carry out the Krebs cycle faster, since it takes place on the cristae.

items.q: Which statement correctly matches an adaptation of the chloroplast to its function in photosynthesis?
items.correct: The thylakoid membranes provide a large surface area in which photosystems are held to absorb light.
items.misconception: The fluid inside the thylakoids contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle at high concentration.
items.why: Thylakoids and grana are the prominent structures in chloroplast diagrams, and 'photosynthesis happens in the thylakoids' is a common simplification, so both stages are assigned to them. The light-dependent reactions take place in the thylakoid membranes. The Calvin cycle is a series of enzyme-catalysed reactions in solution and takes place in the stroma, the fluid surrounding the thylakoids, where its enzymes and substrates are concentrated together.
items.specStatementText: How a chloroplast is built for photosynthesis (HL)
items.random_wrong: The stroma holds the photosystems in solution so that light can reach them from every direction.

items.q: Both mitochondria and chloroplasts produce ATP by chemiosmosis. Which feature of the chloroplast plays the same role as the small intermembrane space of the mitochondrion?
items.correct: The small volume of fluid inside each thylakoid, in which protons accumulate to form a steep gradient quickly.
items.misconception: The large volume of water held inside the thylakoids, which supplies the protons released by photolysis.
items.why: Students learn that photolysis of water takes place in the thylakoid and that the protons it releases accumulate in the thylakoid space, so they infer that the thylakoid must hold a large supply of water to be split, and treat a large internal volume as the adaptation rather than a small one. Thylakoids are flattened sacs enclosing a very small volume. Water is abundant throughout the chloroplast; what the light-dependent reactions need is a compartment small enough for a proton gradient to build up rapidly, which is what the small thylakoid space provides.
items.specStatementText: How a chloroplast is built for photosynthesis (HL)
items.random_wrong: The stroma, in which the photosystems pump protons into the surrounding fluid of the chloroplast.

items.q: A cell is treated with a substance that blocks all of its nuclear pores. Which consequence would follow?
items.correct: mRNA could no longer leave the nucleus, so cytoplasmic ribosomes would receive no new mRNA.
items.misconception: DNA could no longer leave the nucleus to be translated by the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
items.why: Students who have not fully separated DNA from mRNA, and who know that the pores are for getting things out to the ribosomes, conclude that the genetic material itself travels out. DNA remains in the nucleus. The nuclear pores allow mRNA transcribed from DNA to pass out to ribosomes in the cytoplasm, allow ribosomal subunits made in the nucleolus to leave, and allow proteins such as polymerases and histones to enter.
items.specStatementText: Why the nucleus has a double membrane with pores (HL)
items.random_wrong: Protein synthesis would carry on, as ribosomes inside the nucleus would translate the mRNA there.

items.q: What happens to the nuclear membrane during mitosis, and why?
items.correct: It breaks into vesicles so that spindle microtubules can reach the chromosomes.
items.misconception: It pinches into two so that each daughter nucleus keeps part of the original envelope.
items.why: Pre-IB descriptions say 'the nucleus divides', and the visible pinching of the cell in cytokinesis is transferred to the nucleus, so students picture a nucleus splitting like a cell. Spindle microtubules form in the cytoplasm and cannot reach chromosomes enclosed in an intact envelope. The nuclear membrane therefore breaks into vesicles early in mitosis and meiosis, and new envelopes assemble around the two sets of chromosomes after they have been separated. The ability of the double membrane to disassemble into vesicles and reassemble is one of its functional benefits.
items.specStatementText: Why the nucleus has a double membrane with pores (HL)
items.random_wrong: It opens its pores wider so that the chromosomes can pass out into the cytoplasm.

items.q: A pancreatic cell makes the digestive enzyme trypsinogen, which it secretes, and the enzyme hexokinase, which catalyses the first step of glycolysis in its cytoplasm. Where are the two proteins synthesised?
items.correct: Trypsinogen on ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum; hexokinase on free ribosomes lying in the cytoplasm.
items.misconception: Trypsinogen on free ribosomes, which can move to the plasma membrane; hexokinase on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'free' suggests mobility, so students reason that free ribosomes are the ones that can carry proteins to the edge of the cell. 'Free' means not attached to a membrane. Proteins made on free ribosomes are released into the cytoplasm and retained in the cell. Proteins for secretion, or for transport within the cell, are made on membrane-bound ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum and enter the ER lumen as they are synthesised.
items.specStatementText: Free ribosomes and the rough ER (HL)
items.random_wrong: Both on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, from which the hexokinase is later released into the cytoplasm.

items.q: Pancreatic cells were supplied with radioactive amino acids for 3 minutes and then with non-radioactive amino acids. Samples of cells were taken at intervals and the location of radioactive protein was found. After 5 minutes it was mainly in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, after 20 minutes mainly in the Golgi apparatus, and after 60 minutes mainly in vesicles close to the plasma membrane. Which conclusion do these results support?
items.correct: Protein made on the rough ER is passed to the Golgi apparatus for processing and then packaged into secretory vesicles.
items.misconception: Protein flows along a continuous membrane channel from the rough ER, through the Golgi apparatus, to the plasma membrane.
items.why: Diagrams draw the Golgi apparatus lying beside the ER and show arrows from one to the other, so students picture a pipe rather than separate organelles linked by vesicle traffic. The rough ER and the Golgi apparatus are separate compartments. Protein leaves the ER in vesicles, which fuse with the Golgi apparatus; after processing, other vesicles bud from the Golgi apparatus and carry the protein to the plasma membrane. Vesicles are the means of transport between compartments.
items.specStatementText: The Golgi apparatus processes and packages (HL)
items.random_wrong: The Golgi apparatus synthesises the secreted protein, using amino acids that it receives from the rough ER.

items.q: What is the role of clathrin in the formation of a vesicle?
items.correct: It assembles into a lattice on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane, bending it into a pit that pinches off.
items.misconception: It lines the inside of the vesicle so that it can bind and hold the cargo molecules that are being transported.
items.why: The word 'coat' is read as a lining, and students expect the protein that forms the vesicle to be in contact with what the vesicle carries. Clathrin never contacts the cargo. It assembles on the cytoplasmic face of the membrane, forming a cage that pulls the membrane inwards and pinches off the vesicle. Once the vesicle has formed the clathrin coat is shed, leaving a plain membrane that can fuse with its target.
items.specStatementText: Vesicles and clathrin (HL)
items.random_wrong: It is the membrane receptor protein that recognises and binds the substance that is to be brought into the cell.

items.q: A vesicle from the Golgi apparatus carries a protein to the plasma membrane for secretion. What happens to the membrane of the vesicle when the protein is released?
items.correct: It fuses with the plasma membrane and becomes part of it.
items.misconception: It passes out through the plasma membrane and is lost from the cell.
items.why: 'Secretion' suggests something being expelled, and the vesicle is drawn as a ball moving towards the edge of the cell, so students imagine the ball popping out through the membrane. A vesicle cannot pass through a membrane. In exocytosis the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, the contents are released outside the cell, and the vesicle's phospholipids and proteins become part of the plasma membrane. This is also how membrane is added to a growing cell.
items.specStatementText: Vesicles and clathrin (HL)
items.random_wrong: It is broken down into phospholipids reused to build the next vesicle.

items.q: The enzymes and substrates of the Krebs cycle are held together in the mitochondrial matrix rather than being spread through the cytoplasm. Why is this compartmentalization an adaptation for the production of ATP?
items.correct: Enzymes and substrates are concentrated in a small volume, so reactions run rapidly, and reduced NAD is formed close to the inner membrane.
items.misconception: The matrix holds the Krebs cycle enzymes pressed tightly against the cristae, so that they can pump protons directly into the intermembrane space.
items.why: Cristae are the most memorable feature of the mitochondrion, so every process associated with the organelle is assigned to them. The Krebs cycle is a series of enzyme-catalysed reactions in solution and takes place in the matrix. The cristae are folds of the inner membrane that carry the electron transport chain and ATP synthase. Compartmentalizing the Krebs cycle enzymes and substrates in the matrix keeps them concentrated and close to the inner membrane, where the reduced NAD they produce is used.
items.specStatementText: How a mitochondrion is built for ATP (HL)
items.random_wrong: Being enclosed by two membranes protects the Krebs cycle enzymes from being damaged by substances in the rest of the cytoplasm.

items.q: In a chloroplast the enzymes of the Calvin cycle are located in the stroma, while ATP and reduced NADP are produced by the thylakoid membranes. Why is locating the Calvin cycle in the stroma an adaptation for photosynthesis?
items.correct: Enzymes and substrates are concentrated together in the stroma, next to the thylakoids that supply ATP and reduced NADP, so fixation is rapid.
items.misconception: The stroma holds the photosystems in solution, so the Calvin cycle enzymes must be located there too in order to receive light energy directly.
items.why: Pre-IB courses say only that 'chloroplasts contain chlorophyll', and green fluid is easy to imagine, so students picture the pigment in solution rather than embedded in membranes. Photosystems are complexes of pigments and proteins embedded in the thylakoid membranes, together with the electron carriers they pass electrons to. The large surface area of the thylakoid membranes is an adaptation that allows a large number of photosystems to be packed into the chloroplast.
items.specStatementText: How a chloroplast is built for photosynthesis (HL)
items.random_wrong: The Calvin cycle actually takes place inside the thylakoids themselves, and the stroma serves only to store the carbohydrate that the cycle produces.

items.q: Is the cell wall an organelle?
items.correct: No. The cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane and is not a discrete subunit of the cell, so it is not considered an organelle.
items.misconception: The cell wall is an organelle, because it is a labelled structure with a clear function.
items.why: In cell diagrams every labelled structure is treated as 'a part of the cell', and students have learned that structures have functions, so anything with a label and a function is filed as an organelle. Organelles are discrete subunits of cells adapted to specific functions. The cell wall is an extracellular layer secreted by the cell rather than a subunit within it; along with the cytoskeleton and the cytoplasm, it is not considered an organelle.
items.specStatementText: What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the cytoskeleton and the cytoplasm organelles?
items.correct: No. The cytoplasm is the whole internal contents of the cell apart from the nucleus, and the cytoskeleton is a continuous framework running through it; neither is a discrete subunit.
items.misconception: The cytoskeleton and the cytoplasm are organelles, because they are inside the cell and carry out functions.
items.why: Students learn the cytoskeleton as a named structure with functions such as movement and support, and see the cytoplasm listed among cell 'parts', so both are grouped with the organelles they sit alongside. An organelle is a discrete subunit. The cytoplasm is the medium in which organelles are suspended, and the cytoskeleton is a network that extends throughout it, so neither is a separable unit. The guide states that the cell wall, cytoskeleton and cytoplasm are not considered organelles.
items.specStatementText: What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an organelle carry out its function after it has been separated from the cell?
items.correct: Yes, for a time: isolated mitochondria, for example, consume oxygen and make ATP in a suitable solution, which is why cell fractionation allows organelle function to be studied.
items.misconception: Organelles stop working as soon as the cell is broken open, so isolated organelles can only be studied for their structure.
items.why: Cell theory teaches that the cell is the smallest unit of life, and students extend this to mean that nothing smaller than a cell can carry out a life process, even briefly. Organelles are not alive on their own, but the enzymes and membranes they contain keep working after gentle homogenisation in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution. Cell fractionation exploits this: each isolated fraction is tested for the activity it can perform, which is how the functions of organelles were established.
items.specStatementText: What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found

items.q: Why is a cell homogenate spun at a series of increasing speeds rather than once?
items.correct: Because different organelles sediment at different speeds according to their size and density: nuclei pellet at low speed, mitochondria at a higher speed and ribosomes only at very high speed, so a series of speeds separates them.
items.misconception: Centrifuging simply makes everything settle faster, so a single spin gives one pellet containing all the organelles.
items.why: Everyday experience of sediment settling in a liquid suggests that spinning merely speeds up settling; students have no reason to expect that particles of different sizes come down at different speeds. In an ultracentrifuge the force needed to pellet a particle depends on its size and density. At a low speed only the largest, densest organelles (nuclei) form a pellet; the supernatant is then spun faster to pellet mitochondria and chloroplasts, and faster again to bring down small fragments and ribosomes. Each fraction contains mainly one type of organelle, which is what makes studying their separate functions possible.
items.specStatementText: What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found

items.q: Could ribosomes translate DNA directly if they reached it?
items.correct: No. Ribosomes translate mRNA only; DNA must first be transcribed into mRNA. The nuclear membrane separates the site of transcription from the ribosomes, but not because ribosomes could read DNA.
items.misconception: The nucleus keeps ribosomes away from the DNA because ribosomes would otherwise translate the DNA directly.
items.why: Students who think of DNA as 'the code for proteins' skip over the role of mRNA, and then explain the nuclear membrane as a barrier that protects the DNA from being read. Ribosomes bind mRNA, not DNA. The advantage of separating the nucleus from the cytoplasm is that mRNA, once transcribed, can be modified before it meets ribosomes; in prokaryotes, where there is no nucleus, mRNA may immediately meet ribosomes.
items.specStatementText: Why keep the nucleus and cytoplasm apart
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does enclosing a process in a membrane-bound compartment slow it down?
items.correct: No. Concentrating the enzymes and metabolites of a process in a small volume increases the frequency of collisions between enzyme and substrate, so the reactions proceed faster than if the same molecules were spread through the whole cytoplasm.
items.misconception: Compartments slow metabolism, because substances have to cross a membrane to get in and out.
items.why: Membranes are learned first as barriers that control what passes, so a student weighs the cost of crossing the membrane without considering the effect of concentrating the reactants inside it. One advantage of compartmentalization is the concentration of metabolites and enzymes: the same number of molecules in a small compartment gives a much higher concentration, and so a higher reaction rate, than in the whole cytoplasm. Transport proteins in the compartment membrane move substrates and products across it.
items.specStatementText: Why compartments help the cytoplasm
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the function of the mitochondrion's double membrane?
items.correct: The inner membrane holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase and is folded into cristae; the outer membrane bounds the organelle, and between the two lies the small intermembrane space into which protons are pumped.
items.misconception: The double membrane is there to give the mitochondrion extra protection or strength.
items.why: Membranes are introduced as boundaries that 'protect' the cell, so a second membrane is read as a second layer of protection rather than as the creation of an additional compartment. The two membranes are functionally different. The inner membrane is the site of electron transport and ATP synthesis, and having a second, outer membrane creates the intermembrane space, a small compartment in which a proton gradient can build up. The double membrane is an adaptation for producing ATP, not for protection.
items.specStatementText: How a mitochondrion is built for ATP (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does the nuclear envelope need pores?
items.correct: Because large molecules such as mRNA, ribosomal subunits and proteins cannot pass through the phospholipid bilayers of the envelope; pores provide channels through both membranes.
items.misconception: Substances move between the nucleus and cytoplasm by diffusing through the nuclear membranes, in the same way as small molecules cross the plasma membrane.
items.why: Membrane transport is learned first through diffusion and osmosis of small molecules, so students assume that anything can diffuse across a membrane if there is a concentration gradient. Phospholipid bilayers are impermeable to large, polar molecules such as RNA and proteins. Nuclear pores are needed so that mRNA and ribosomal subunits can leave the nucleus and proteins such as polymerases and histones can enter it; without them the nucleus could not communicate with the cytoplasm.
items.specStatementText: Why the nucleus has a double membrane with pores (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all of a cell's proteins made on the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
items.correct: No. Proteins that will function in the cytoplasm or nucleus are made on free ribosomes; only proteins for transport within the cell, membrane insertion or secretion are made on the rough ER.
items.misconception: All protein synthesis takes place on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
items.why: Diagrams of the cell usually show ribosomes only as dots along the rough ER, and the rough ER is described as 'the site of protein synthesis', so free ribosomes are overlooked. Most of the ribosomes in many cells are free in the cytoplasm. A cell uses two populations of ribosomes for two destinations: free ribosomes for proteins retained in the cell and membrane-bound ribosomes on the rough ER for proteins that will be transported within the cell or secreted.
items.specStatementText: Free ribosomes and the rough ER (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the Golgi apparatus synthesise proteins?
items.correct: No. It processes proteins that were synthesised on the rough endoplasmic reticulum and packages them into vesicles for secretion or for transport within the cell.
items.misconception: The Golgi apparatus makes the proteins that the cell secretes.
items.why: The Golgi apparatus is described as 'producing' or 'preparing' secretory products, and students merge this with production of the protein itself. The Golgi apparatus has no ribosomes, so it cannot synthesise protein. It receives protein from the rough ER in vesicles, modifies it and sorts it into vesicles that bud from the far face of the stack; those vesicles carry the protein to the plasma membrane for secretion.
items.specStatementText: The Golgi apparatus processes and packages (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is clathrin the receptor that binds the substance taken into a vesicle?
items.correct: No. Receptors in the membrane bind the substance; clathrin is a coat protein on the cytoplasmic side that shapes the membrane into a vesicle.
items.misconception: Clathrin is the membrane receptor that recognises the material to be brought into the cell.
items.why: In receptor-mediated endocytosis both the receptor and clathrin are mentioned together, and clathrin is the only protein named, so it is assumed to be the one doing the recognising. Clathrin does not bind cargo. Its role is structural: it assembles into a lattice beneath the membrane, bends it into a pit and helps it pinch off. Recognition of the cargo, where it occurs, is the job of separate receptor proteins in the membrane.
items.specStatementText: Vesicles and clathrin (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the membrane of a new vesicle come from?
items.correct: It is a piece of an existing membrane, such as the plasma membrane, the ER or the Golgi apparatus, that has budded off.
items.misconception: A vesicle's membrane is made from scratch around its contents and broken down again after delivery.
items.why: Vesicles appear and disappear in diagrams, so students assume they are built and dismantled rather than budded from one membrane and merged into another. Vesicles form by budding: a region of membrane, shaped by clathrin, pinches off enclosing its contents. When the vesicle fuses with a target membrane its bilayer joins that membrane. Membrane is therefore transferred from one compartment to another, not made and destroyed for each vesicle.
items.specStatementText: Vesicles and clathrin (HL)
